head:
Health · Eating disorders

When sport is not the first step: anorexia and eating disorders

On this site, almost every article tells you to move more. This one says something else: for some people, that is not the right starting point, and the first step is to get care. It deliberately contains no programme, no dose, no numerical target.

If this concerns you, or if you are worried about someone

Talk to your GP, or to a health professional you trust. It is never too late to seek help.6

National helpline Anorexie Boulimie Info Écoute, anonymous, run by the Fédération française anorexie boulimie (FFAB): 09 69 32 59 00, not a premium-rate number, from 16h to 18h on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday.12,13,14

In case of immediate danger or serious illness: call 15 or 112.13

The question

You may already have read, here or elsewhere, that exercise is good for almost everything: the heart, mood, sleep. That is true in general. But "in general" does not mean "for everyone, at every moment". There are situations where the same activity that helps most people sustains suffering. Eating disorders, and anorexia nervosa in particular, are among them.

It is also an area where a well-intentioned article can do harm. A training plan, a test to repeat, a progression target, a ranking: each of these tools, useful for many people, can become fuel for the illness in a vulnerable person. So this article does the opposite of what you expect from a coaching article. It explains why no plan is given here, what the research says, how to recognise that something is wrong, and who should decide the place of exercise.

The question

When a person has anorexia or another eating disorder, what can be said that is accurate about exercise without harming them, and who should decide its place?

The answer comes in four steps: how common the problem is among athletes, the mechanism of energy deficiency, what research knows about exercise in eating disorders, then the limits of that knowledge. After that come the warning signs, the care response, what this site must forbid itself, and what those close to the person can do.

What is at stake

What is at stake is first of all physical and psychological health. Anorexia nervosa is a serious illness that requires coordinated care: the recommendations of the Haute Autorité de santé (HAS) describe follow-up that covers the nutritional, somatic, psychological and family dimensions.5 The earlier it is identified, the better the prognosis: the HAS says so in the same document.5

There is then an issue specific to sport. Sport can hide a disorder, because a very active person is seen as "disciplined" or "motivated". It can also sustain it. And it can be the place where the people around, a coach, a training partner, are the first to see the changes. The HAS notes, moreover, that professionals and people in contact with at-risk groups, including sports coaches, are well placed to spot it early.5

Finally, there is an issue for a site like this one. Fitness tests, repeated measurements, norm tables: all of this can help someone find their place, or become an obsession. We need to know where the page stops.

Step 1 of 4 · How common it is among athletes

Eating disorders are more common in elite athletes, especially in certain sports

We start from the broadest finding. In a Norwegian study that has become a classic, researchers followed almost all of the country's elite athletes (1,620) and a control group (1,696). A first phase by questionnaire identified the people at risk, then a clinical interview determined who met the criteria for an eating disorder, including in a partial form ("subclinical").3

Among elite athletes, these disorders are about three times as common as in the control group

Source: Sundgot-Borgen and Torstveit, Norwegian athletes, source 3. Both heights are drawn to the same scale. The "about three times" is a ratio calculated from these two values (13.5 divided by 4.6, so derived). Association study, conducted in Norway: it does not say that sport causes the disorder.

What this means

An eating disorder is an illness that is more widespread in elite sport than in the general population. The HAS also writes this for anorexia.5 That does not mean that doing sport makes you ill. It means that the sporting environment must be a place of vigilance, not only of performance.

The risk is not evenly distributed. In the same study, among women, the share of people affected was higher in sports where appearance or weight matter (so-called aesthetic sports), and also higher in endurance sports than in ball sports.3

The risk varies greatly with the type of sport

Source: Sundgot-Borgen and Torstveit, source 3. Scale: 10 pixels per 1%. The abstract that was read does not give a statistical test for this comparison between sports in women. In men, the same study also finds differences between sports.

What this means

The more a sport combines performance and control of the body, the higher the risk. A synthesis of seven studies points the same way: six of them find more eating disorders in sports where thinness is valued.4 If you train in endurance sports, this is not a reason to worry, it is a reason to know.

This step establishes that the problem is real and that sport is not immune to it. What remains is to understand by what mechanism sport and eating can become entangled to the point of harming each other.

Step 2 of 4 · The mechanism

Exercise requires energy: when it is lacking, the whole body pays

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) named this mechanism in a consensus statement: RED-S, for "Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport". The idea is simple. The body needs a certain amount of energy to function, in addition to what exercise uses up. When intake does not cover the whole, this is called low energy availability. The IOC defines RED-S as impaired physiological functioning caused by this relative deficiency.1

This deficiency can be intentional or not. It can come from an eating disorder, but also from simple lack of attention: expenditure that rises without eating keeping up. That is why the concept is useful: it does not require judging an intention.

The 2018 consensus lists the systems affected: hormonal, menstrual, bone, metabolic, blood, cardiovascular, digestive, immune, psychological. On the performance side, it cites more frequent illness and injuries, slower recovery, and altered mood and concentration.1 In other words, lack of energy does not make you progress: it makes you regress, including in the sport you wanted to serve.

In women, an older framework describes three linked elements: low energy availability with or without an eating disorder, menstrual cycle disorders, and bone fragility. This is the "female athlete triad", taken up in a 2014 consensus statement on treatment and return to play.2

What this means

A body that trains without receiving enough energy does not get stronger. It wears down. And the first signs are not always visible from the outside: a cycle that changes, injuries that keep coming back, fatigue that does not go away. The IOC says this for men too: runners, cyclists, rowers and weight-category sports are cited among those most concerned.1

So far, we have seen that the problem exists and that it has a mechanism. What remains is the question that this site must treat with the most caution: what does research say about exercise in people who have an eating disorder?

Step 3 of 4 · What research says about exercise in eating disorders

The evidence is scarce, small and drawn from supervised care

In eating disorders, physical activity has two faces. On one side, compulsive exercise: activity that takes up all the space, that is pursued despite fatigue or injury, and whose cessation causes distress. The DSM-5 describes, in anorexia, increased energy expenditure through excessive exercise.7 The HAS speaks of physical hyperactivity, described in certain forms, and of often very marked perfectionism.5 A 2023 review reports that this dysfunctional exercise is present in 22 to 80% of people who have an eating disorder, a very wide range, which mainly reflects different definitions between studies.11

On the other side, a question that clinicians ask themselves: should all activity be forbidden during treatment, or can it find a place there, very closely supervised? The reviews that have looked at this point are few.

The evidence base is thin: a few studies, often small

Sources: source 8 (CRD register record) and source 9 (summary of the review). Scale: 40 pixels per study. In the 2008 review, more than 375 participants in total; three studies of only 14 to 21 people.

Hausenblas, Cook and Chittester (2008). This review brought together six studies. Its authors conclude that exercise "may improve a range of outcomes" in patients with an eating disorder, but that more research is needed. The CRD register reviewers note that the validity of the studies was not fully assessed and that the method is incompletely described.8

Moola and colleagues (2013). Systematic review on anorexia: 1,664 articles found, 10 retained (5 randomised trials, 2 quasi-experimental studies, 2 case studies, 1 qualitative study). No study reported a negative effect on weight. In the only two studies that measured the symptoms of the disorder, neither showed a worsening, and six studies out of ten reported better well-being. The authors conclude that adapted and safe physical activity "does no harm" while offering benefits, but they specify that the studies are few, small, often poorly described, that simultaneous psychological care was not controlled, that publication bias was not assessed and that disorders other than anorexia were excluded.9

Quesnel (2018). A piece of work carried out at the University of British Columbia, Okanagan, published in the journal Eating Disorders, is based on interviews with professionals in these disorders in North America and Europe. It suggests that the abrupt and complete cessation of all activity during treatment is perhaps less effective than is believed, and calls for individualised and gradual guidance. It is not a trial, it is expert opinion: the press release read for this article gives neither the number of interviewees nor the method.10 The same author then co-signed, in 2023, a review of the medical complications of exercise in eating disorders: it lists the situations where exercise may be contraindicated or must be modified, and presents itself as a resource for care teams, not as a guide for people on their own.11

What this means

What is demonstrated is very limited. The reviews describe adapted, supervised programmes, within care, and nothing more. They do not say that a person with anorexia should start on their own, nor that it would be risk-free outside follow-up. They say only that no evidence was found that activity, properly supervised, makes things worse, and that the question deserves better studies.

Step 4 of 4 · The limits of this knowledge

What the studies do not allow us to conclude

The most important point of this article fits in one sentence: the absence of evidence of danger in small supervised studies is not evidence of safety outside a supervised setting. Several reasons add up.

The populations and the contexts differ. The studies describe people followed by a team, sometimes hospitalised, with adaptations decided by clinicians. The setting is part of the intervention.

The samples are small and publication bias is possible. The reviews say so themselves.8,9

We do not know for whom, when, or how far. The 2023 review lists situations where exercise may be contraindicated or require modifications, for example depending on heart condition, blood pressure or hydration.11 Only a team that knows the person can judge this.

And the athlete? The IOC is clear: an athlete who meets the criteria for a severe disorder such as anorexia or bulimia should not take part in competition, exercise may need to be reduced or stopped depending on severity, and treatment must be provided by a multidisciplinary team. The IOC also specifies that these recommendations "require further validation".1 The 2014 statement on the triad adds that the decision to return is taken by the physician, with the team.2

One last point of caution about screening tools: the IOC notes that none of the questionnaires for screening eating disorders used in athletes has been validated against DSM-5 criteria.1 An online score therefore does not replace a consultation.

The warning signs

What follows is not a diagnostic tool. Only a professional can make a diagnosis. These are reasons to talk about it. To limit risks, no specific eating behaviour is described here: we describe what can be seen in the person's life.

What those around the person or the coach may notice

  • A marked physical change, or periods without menstruation. The HAS cites weight loss, menstrual disorders and disturbances of body image among the warning signs.5
  • A practice that takes up all the space, that continues despite injury, illness or fatigue, with anxiety or guilt when it is prevented.
  • Injuries that follow one another, lasting fatigue, faintness, constantly feeling cold, a mood that darkens or becomes irritable.
  • Withdrawal from meals and shared moments, a new rigidity around eating, secrecy.
  • A constant preoccupation with the body, with performance or with comparison to others.

What the person may notice themselves

  • Exercise is no longer a pleasure but an obligation that you can no longer do without.
  • Thinking about eating and about the body takes up a large part of the day.
  • You hide, you play things down, or you feel guilty without a clear reason.

The HAS recommends, for front-line professionals, a short screening questionnaire (the SCOFF-F), which detects a possible disorder and not a diagnosis: a positive result leads to a specialist referral.5 The GP is the right way in.

What this means

A single sign proves nothing. But several together, or a single one that lasts, justify asking for an opinion. Better a consultation "for nothing" than a disorder spotted too late.

The response: care first, sport afterwards, on the advice of the care team

This is the part that replaces the "implementation" of the other articles. It is not a programme: it is a care pathway, and every step belongs to professionals.

  1. Talk about itTo a trusted person, then to a doctor. The HAS insists on early action: early identification prevents symptoms from becoming established.5,6
  2. See the GPThe GP first looks for signs of immediate severity, then coordinates or refers to a specialist colleague.7
  3. Enter coordinated careA multidisciplinary team: a mental health professional and a somatic physician at minimum, according to Vidal's summary of the HAS recommendations; care covers the nutritional, somatic, psychological and family dimensions.5,7 In sport, the statement on the triad adds the sports physician, a sports dietitian, and sometimes the coach and the family.2
  4. Let the team decide on activityResuming, adapting or suspending sport is a medical, individual decision, and it changes over time. It is not made alone, nor on a website.1,2

Patient and family associations, as well as the helpline mentioned above, can help with taking the first two steps, anonymously. The HAS itself mentions this possibility.6

Who this site is for, and what a test page must not do here

THW offers fitness tests: endurance, strength, mobility. For the great majority of people, measuring your starting point and repeating it from time to time is useful. For a person with an eating disorder, it is not the right tool, and the site must say so clearly.

  • No test in this situation. If this article concerns you, do not take this site's tests. Talk first to a health professional.
  • No obsessive measurement. No injunction to repeat a test, no streak of days to maintain, no reminder that makes you feel guilty for an absence.
  • No ranking. No podium, no comparison between users, no "top": comparison is fuel for the disorder.
  • No measuring the body as a goal. The tests assess what the body can do. They must not become surveillance of its appearance or composition.
  • A referral to care. A banner on every test page leads to this article and to the helpline.

And if you are a coach or trainer: this article is not written so that you "manage" a disorder, but so that you know how to refer. You do not have to make a diagnosis; you have to say what you see, gently, and refer to a doctor.

What those close to the person can do

The HAS fact sheets on "how to talk about it" give guidance that can be taken up.6 They concern bulimia and binge eating disorder, but the communication principles are common sense for all eating disorders.

  • Understand that it is not a lack of willpower. These are disorders that require care.
  • Look at the whole person. Talk about what they are going through (fatigue, sadness, withdrawal) rather than only about what they eat or about their body, which will put them on the defensive.
  • Value their strengths and their efforts rather than pointing out failures or relapses.
  • Give hope without dramatising. Recovery is possible despite the length of the disorders and possible relapses.
  • Anticipate the obstacles. Shame, fear of judgement, denial and the cost of care are real obstacles. Offer to go with them to an appointment.
  • Do not play the carer. No surveillance, no control, no bargaining over sport: the HAS notes that excessive family control can get in the way of care.5
  • Look after yourself. Those close to the person also have resources: the helpline is also for them.

Answer to the question

The question was: what can be said that is accurate about sport when a person has anorexia, and who decides its place?

What is solid. Eating disorders are more common in elite athletes, especially in sports where the body is controlled. Lack of energy affects many systems of the body. The HAS recommendations and international consensus statements call for coordinated care with a team, and make the return to sport a medical decision.

What is probable but limited. Within care, adapted activity was not found to be harmful in small studies, and total cessation is debated. But these studies are few, small, and do not concern practice outside of care.

What is not demonstrated. That a person can safely resume sport alone, or that a generic programme, a dose or a test is appropriate. No source read shows it. That is why this article contains no plan, no dose and no target.

The answer therefore comes down to two words: get care. Sport may come back, often, but in the place and at the pace that the care team sets.

Limits of this article
  • It does not replace medical advice or follow-up. It is not personalised advice.
  • Quesnel's 2018 work was read only through its press release; the 2008 and 2013 reviews were read through records and summaries, not in full text.
  • The 2019 HAS recommendations concern bulimia and binge eating disorder, those of 2010 concern anorexia nervosa. The HAS advice for those close to the person is taken from the fact sheet on bulimia.
  • The frequency figures come from an older Norwegian study, on elite athletes; they cannot be transposed as they are to recreational sport.

Frequently asked questions

I do sport and I am worried about my relationship with my body. What should I do?

Make an appointment with your GP, and tell them precisely what worries you. You can also call the helpline, anonymously. Do not try to test yourself or to correct yourself alone.

My child, my pupil or my training partner has changed. Should I talk to them about it?

Yes, and without waiting to be certain. Talk about what you see and what you feel, with kindness, without blame, without talking about weight or food. Offer to go with them to a doctor.

Should all sport be stopped in the case of an eating disorder?

It is not for an article to say. Specialists themselves discuss the place of activity in care. The decision rests with the care team, case by case.

Why is there no test to take on this page?

Because for a vulnerable person, repeated measurement and numerical benchmarks can feed the illness. We prefer that this site does not set this trap.

No protocol on this page

Unlike the other articles, this content does not come before a test. See the editorial note: it is offered on the "Before you start" page and as a banner on the test pages, never as the introduction to a protocol to be completed.

Editorial note (does not appear on the site).

Helpline number: to be settled before publication. The number provided in the request, 0 810 037 037, is the one in the HAS fact sheet of June 2019 and in an old AP-HP document (0.06 € per minute plus the price of the call). Two more recent sources give 09 69 32 59 00, not a premium-rate number: a 2023 article on the FFAB campaign and the Qare page. The FFAB site and the World Day site could not be opened; the article therefore displays the most recent number, but it must be checked on ffab.fr before publication. Hours: Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday from 16h to 18h (2023 article and Find A Helpline record, which specifies that Wednesday is excluded); the older sources say Monday to Friday.

Content choices. No plan, dose, duration, target, weight, BMI, calorie, or description of method. The "implementation" is a care pathway. No test to repeat. No typical character: a fictional case would have required describing behaviours. The figures were rechecked on an open page, except those marked below. The only percentage figures kept: frequency (13.5 and 4.6; 42, 24, 17, 16; range 22-80%), which do not describe behaviours.

Derived figures. "About three times" (13.5 divided by 4.6, i.e. 2.9); heights of the bars proportional to the values read.

Not verified or to be qualified. (1) Sundgot-Borgen and Torstveit 2004: the abstract read (qxmd) gives neither authors nor year; the attribution comes from the title. (2) Mancine 2020: abstract only (7 studies, 6 out of 7); no percentage reproduced. (3) Hausenblas 2008: CRD record, not the article. (4) Moola 2013: Mental Elf summary; authors, journal and exact number of participants not reproduced. (5) Quesnel 2018: press release only; the release speaks of 30 to 80% dysfunctional exercise, the article uses the range from the 2023 review (22 to 80%), read on the truncated publisher page; final recommendations of that review not read. (6) Vidal 2025: secondary article summarising the HAS; "at least two clinicians" is taken from this summary and relates to the 2019 recommendations (bulimia), not to those of 2010 on anorexia. (7) HAS 2010: extracts of the argumentaire only; the section on physical activity and its resumption was not found in the extracts read, so nothing is attributed to the HAS on this subject. (8) Triad 2014: severity threshold (body mass index) read but deliberately not reproduced. (9) The IOC guidance on competition is that of the BJSM page read, which specifies that it must be further validated. (10) 2022 review on exercise therapy in anorexia (PMC9627498): not opened, not cited. PubMed and PMC often block access.

Removed. The medical thresholds of the 2023 review (numerical values for weight and heart rate, excluded by safeguard), the list of screening tests and their questions (SCOFF-F cited without the detail), the severity figures of the triad, the male data by sport, the "30 to 80%" quotation from the press release.

To be decided by the founder. (a) Placement: I recommend not displaying this article above a test protocol, but on the "Before you start" page and as a permanent referral banner on every test. (b) Review by a professional (doctor or psychologist specialising in eating disorders) before publication: I strongly recommend it, this is a subject where an error can cause harm. (c) Whether or not to add 3114 (national suicide prevention number): not read at the source here, so not written. (d) Title: "When sport is not the first step" is the requested title; the subtitle could be just "anorexia and eating disorders", to be discussed.
